one_liner: Header-only C++ binary serializer that reflects plain structs at compile time, no .proto or macros; ~2-20x faster than protobuf.
what_it_does: struct_pack turns C++ aggregates, std containers, optional/variant/expected and unique_ptr into a compact binary buffer and back. There is no IDL, code generator or per-type boilerplate: `struct_pack::serialize(obj)` returns a std::vector<char> (or any buffer type you name, or writes to a stream or raw pointer), and `struct_pack::deserialize<T>(buf)` returns an expected<T, err_code>. It does not replace protobuf on the wire. The format is its own (a 4-byte type hash, then fields in close to their native layout), so both ends must be C++ builds that share the struct definitions. Non-aggregate types need a YLT_REFL(type, fields...) macro, and any field added later must be declared as struct_pack::compatible<T, version>.
how_it_is_fast: The field list comes from compile-time aggregate reflection: it counts members by probing brace-initialization with a type that converts to anything (the Boost.PFR/magic_get trick). All type dispatch is resolved in templates, so per-field code is inlined with no virtual calls or runtime schema walk, and the type check is an MD5 hash computed at compile time, so the runtime check is one 32-bit compare. Trivially copyable structs, and contiguous containers of them, are written and read with a single memcpy on little-endian hosts. Serialize first computes the exact output size, grows the buffer once (skipping zero-fill through a private-member hack on libstdc++, libc++ and MSVC STL), then writes through an unchecked pointer, with one length-prefix width (1/2/4/8 bytes) chosen per message from the largest container.
when_to_use: C++-to-C++ messaging or persistence where both sides compile the same struct definitions: RPC between your own services, cache blobs, snapshots. It is the wire format of the same repo's coro_rpc.

Payloads that are mostly trivially copyable data (POD structs, std::vector/std::array of PODs). These become one memcpy, which is where the ~16-20x serialize gap over protobuf appears (the 20-rect case).
Hot paths that serialize small-to-medium nested structs with strings, vectors and enums, where protobuf's generated serialize/parse took ~2-5x longer in the project's person and Monster cases.
Codebases that want serialization without a protoc step, IDL files or hand-written serialize() functions, on C++17 or newer (tested down to GCC 9.1, Clang 6, MSVC 19.20).
Reading one field from a large blob (get_field<T, I>()), or zero-copy deserialization into std::string_view/std::span members pointing into a buffer you keep alive.
when_not_to_use: You need cross-language readers, schema files for other teams, or protobuf wire compatibility. The documented implementation is C++ only (the same repo's struct_pb handles protobuf-format C++ structs without protoc).

Bandwidth- or storage-bound traffic of small integers. Integers are fixed-width by default, so 20 rects encode to ~325 B vs ~255 B for protobuf and ~220 B for msgpack in the project's own size chart, and msgpack is also smaller for Monsters (~1,540 B vs ~1,830 B). Turn on ENCODING_WITH_VARINT/USE_FAST_VARINT or pick a varint format.

Schemas that change in ways other than appending fields. You may not delete, reorder or retype fields, compatible<T, version> numbers must strictly increase (otherwise the docs call the result undefined behavior), and compatible fields inside structs held in containers or unordered_maps had data-corruption and 'not supported' bugs fixed only in 2025-2026 (issues #1026, #1167).

Parsing hostile input where you need a proven hardened decoder. Reads are bounds-checked (they return no_buffer_space) and stream reads cap unconfirmed preallocation at 1 MB, but the repo has no fuzz tests, and in release mode the type check is only a 31-bit hash, which the docs say leads to undefined behavior on collision.
Big-endian targets. Data is always stored little-endian, so the memcpy fast paths are off for multi-byte types there, and the docs say performance is lower.

integration.dependencies: none for struct_pack itself, but it needs the bundled include/ylt/reflection headers and include/ylt/util/expected.hpp. Packaged for vcpkg, Homebrew, CMake FetchContent/add_subdirectory and Bazel. The asio/async_simple dependencies of the monorepo apply only to its RPC/HTTP libraries.
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (tested minimums GCC 9.1, Clang 6.0, MSVC 19.20/VS2019). C++20 also memcpy's user-defined trivial contiguous containers. CI runs GCC 11.2, Clang 14, AppleClang 14 and MSVC 19.33.
integration.platforms: any: little- and big-endian, 32- and 64-bit (memcpy fast paths only on little-endian). CI runs on Ubuntu, macOS and Windows.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. The API is stateless free functions over caller-owned objects and buffers, and the only static state seen in unpacker.hpp is thread_local, so concurrent calls on distinct buffers appear safe.

gotchas: Debug and release builds write different bytes. Debug embeds the full type-name string to catch hash collisions, while release stores only the hash. If DISABLE_META_INFO is set on one side it must be set on the other, or behavior is undefined.

Trivially copyable structs go out in their in-memory layout, padding included. The type hash covers alignment, so an alignas/#pragma pack mismatch fails cleanly instead of misreading, but #pragma pack users must also specialize struct_pack::pack_alignment<T> (and struct_pack::alignment<T> when combined with alignas).

Buffers are resized without zero-fill by writing private members of std::string/std::vector<char> (string_thief/vector_thief), with a fallback to resize() under ASan. This caused random MSVC crashes with std::wstring (issue #630, fixed 2024), and an MSVC-only bug copied data between map entries of types with a user-defined copy assignment (issue #1140, fixed Dec 2025).

Errors come back as struct_pack::err_code or expected<T, err_code> (a breaking change in Jan 2024); the only throw is std::runtime_error for an unknown struct_pack_id when serializing a polymorphic unique_ptr<base>. Reflection is capped at 256 fields (124 for YLT_REFL on MSVC without /Zc:preprocessor), and very large structs have overflowed small debug stacks (issue #1132, fixed Dec 2025).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick struct_pack over FBE (the other protobuf-baseline entry) when both ends are C++ and you want no domain-model/codegen step; FBE generates code for 9 languages. Pick it over bitsery when you don't want to write a serialize(S&, T&) function per type. Prefer Cista++ for in-place access to mmapped data and libFuzzer-checked parsing, or bitsery for the smallest payloads. struct_pack's edge over Cista++ is that it works on std::string, std::vector and other std containers directly rather than Cista's own data:: types.
verified_claims_summary: Project bar charts measured on Alibaba Clang 13 on a Xeon Platinum 8163 @ 2.5 GHz, in a CMake Release build with STRUCT_PACK_OPTIMIZE, show average time for a vector of 20 objects against protobuf's SerializeToString/ParseFromString. Serialize is ~16-20x faster for 20 four-int rects (~15-20 ns vs ~325 ns), ~5x for persons and ~4.4x for Monsters; deserialize is ~5x, ~2.2x and ~2.3x faster (Monsters ~7.6 µs vs ~17.5 µs). Values are read from PNGs, and the benchmark committed when the charts were added used 100,000 iterations and a 3-character name ("tom", consistent with the ~400 B size chart), whereas the page says one million and today's code uses a 1,024-char name.
status_note: Actively maintained: last commit 2026-09-21, release 0.6.1 in April 2026, Apache-2.0. struct_pack is header-only and can be vendored with its reflection and util headers, but it ships inside a large multi-library monorepo and had schema-evolution fixes as recently as April 2026.
